notes:
I've written notes for every verse, but some parts of your brief went unmet:

- **Catholic, Orthodox and debated popular teaching:** I found nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or netbible.org, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those sections are left out.
- **Protestant traditions:** the pages I read don't show the traditions taking clearly different sides on this chapter. Where commentators disagree, the split crosses tradition lines. I've marked those spots "Debated" and named the commentator.
- **Wording:** most older sources comment on the KJV, so their phrases ("desert of the sea," "a lion," "anoint the shield") differ from the BSB.

---

**v. 1 – "Desert by the Sea"**
- Guzik: Babylon is called this because its plain was broken up by lakes and marshes, which were spoken of as a "sea." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-21/
- Gill: "Desert" is a play on the word, since Babylon was fertile. The word may mean "plain," because Babylon was built on one. Poole instead takes "desert" as a prophecy that the busy city would become a wasteland. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-1.htm
- Barnes: Whirlwinds in Scripture often come from the south. The deserts of Arabia lay south of Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-1.htm
- Ellicott: The verb has no stated subject, which makes the opening vague and frightening. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-1.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: The title phrase appears nowhere else in the Bible, so it doubts Isaiah wrote it. It suggests that what "comes" is the "dire vision" of verse 2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm

**v. 2 – Elam and Media**
- Guzik: Elam and Media are ancient names for the peoples of Persia. Isaiah sees the Persian armies marching on Babylon ahead of time. He quotes Trapp that God often uses one tyrant to punish another. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-21/
- Pulpit: Cyrus held the title "King of Ansan," probably part of Elam. Isaiah used a name his hearers knew. The "groaning" that ends is the suffering Babylon caused to nations and captives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Coke: The groaning may be either the weary Medes and Persians or the captive Jews who were freed when the city fell. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/isaiah-21.html
- *Modern scholarship:* Utley (bible.org) says this is not the later Babylon of Nebuchadnezzar but Isaiah's own Chaldeans under Merodach-baladan, whom Sargon II defeated. He notes the cries to Elam and Media could be war cries of an anti-Assyrian alliance. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-21
- The Expositor's Bible (1887) likewise reads the chapter as Babylon falling to Sargon of Assyria. https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/nvl/isaiah/21-8.html
- The Pulpit Commentary calls the Sargon view "absolutely fatal" because Assyria is never mentioned. It holds that this is Cyrus's capture of Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm

**vv. 3–4 – The prophet's anguish**
- Pulpit: The prophet is horrified at the carnage he sees. The tone is sympathy, not triumph. "The twilight of my desire" means the night he usually spent in peaceful rest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Utley asks why Isaiah would be so upset. He suggests the violence itself, or that Babylon's fall freed Assyria to expand. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-21
- Guzik quotes Trapp: nothing is more hopeless than a wicked man in distress. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-21/

**v. 5 – The feast and "oil the shields"**
- Pulpit: Babylon feasts as though there were no danger. It is "impossible not to think" of Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5). Shields were oiled so weapons would slide off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Barnes agrees the table is Belshazzar's feast. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-5.html
- *Debated – who is told to arise?*
  - Gill and Poole say the call is to the Median and Persian princes to attack while Babylon feasts. Poole says most commentators read it this way.
  - Keil & Delitzsch and JFB say it is the surprised Babylonian revellers being called to defend themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-5.htm
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) says the link to Belshazzar's feast looks "very questionable" on closer study. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-5.html
- Clarke reports a Jewish reading in which "anoint the shield" means "anoint a new king" after Belshazzar's death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-5.html

**vv. 6–7 – The lookout**
- Pulpit:
  - Because Isaiah posts a watchman who waits a long time, the fulfilment seems far off.
  - The riders are cavalry in pairs, not chariots.
  - The donkeys and camels are baggage animals the Persians used.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Matthew Henry: the donkey and camel seem to stand for the Medes and Persians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-1.htm

**v. 8 – The watchman's cry**
- Pulpit: The KJV's "A lion" means he cried like a lion, loudly. He is complaining to God about his long watch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Clarke thinks the Hebrew text is miscopied and should read "the seer." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-8.html
- Barnes compares the scene to the watchman waiting for Troy's fall in Aeschylus's *Agamemnon*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-8.html

**v. 9 – "Fallen, fallen is Babylon"**
- Guzik: Fulfilled when the Medes and Persians conquered Babylon. The repeated "fallen" ties it to Revelation 18:2 and the end-time judgment of the world system. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-21/
- Barnes: the repetition stresses certainty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-9.html
- Calvin: the speaker cannot be Belshazzar's own watchman. The prophet announces what God will do. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-9.html
- *Debated – the broken idols:*
  - Pulpit: Cyrus did not destroy Babylon's idols; he honoured them. The gods were shattered morally, not physically.
  
    https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
  - Heaster, a Christadelphian, takes this as a part not literally fulfilled and moves it to the last days (Revelation 18). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-9.html

**v. 10 – "Crushed on the threshing floor"**
- Pulpit: Israel's sufferings thresh grain from chaff. The message comforts those who come through as pure wheat (compare Matthew 3:12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Matthew Henry: true believers are God's grain and must expect to be threshed by afflictions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-1.htm

**v. 11 – Dumah and Seir**
- Pulpit:
  - "Dumah" means "silence." It is a wordplay for Edom, pointing to coming ruin.
  - Neither town called Dumah lies in Seir.
  - The call may be imagined, not a real embassy.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Ellicott links Dumah to the silence of the grave. The Geneva Bible makes it an Ishmaelite city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-11.htm
- Guzik calls it a "vague, mysterious" burden. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-21/
- *Debated – is the caller sincere?*
  - Matthew Henry treats the question as a serious one from someone more concerned than the careless people around him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/21-11.html
  - Ironside hears a sceptical tone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/isaiah-21.html
  - The *Homilist* sermon calls it sarcastic. https://biblehub.com/sermons/isaiah/21-11.htm
- Spurgeon turns the question into a devotional for the church: watch for error and sin, and look for Christ's coming. https://www.blueletterbible.org/devotionals/me/view.cfm?doy=219&Time=both

**v. 12 – "Morning has come, but also the night"**
- *Debated – what the answer means:*
  - Pulpit: a brief brighter time for Edom, then renewed misery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
  - Barnes: morning for the captive Jews, night for the Edomites. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-12.htm
  - Cambridge Bible: the obscurity is deliberate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-12.htm
  - Wolf, quoted by Guzik: Assyria's night ends, a short morning follows, then Babylon's night. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-21/
- *Lutheran:* Keil & Delitzsch say Luther "hit upon it": when morning comes it will still be night. They trace a series of empires, each dawn swallowed by a new night. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-12.htm
- *Debated – is "come back" a call to repent?*
  - Barnes, JFB, Gill and Poole (if Isaiah is the watchman) say yes.
  - Ellicott says there is not enough evidence. Cambridge says it is "impossible" and renders it "come again." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-12.htm
- Gill (Baptist) reads it through church history: the Gospel's morning, then darkness, the Reformation, then a coming night before Christ's reign. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-12.htm
- Matthew Henry: make good use of today's morning, because night follows. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/21-12.htm

**v. 13 – Dedanite caravans**
- Pulpit: Read "in Arabia," meaning only some northern tribes. "Thickets" means scrub, not forest. The trading caravans must leave the road and hide. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Utley says it is unclear who the attacker is: Assyria, or a civil war. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-21

**vv. 14–15 – Tema and the refugees**
- Pulpit: Tema's people are urged to bring water to the fleeing Dedanites. Kay thinks they were already feeding them. The attacker was probably Assyria, though no record of this war has been found. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
- Guzik pictures them as thirsty refugees fleeing the sword. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-21/

**vv. 16–17 – Kedar within a year**
- Guzik: the attack would come soon after Isaiah spoke. He quotes Poole: "as a hired worker would count it" means an exact year, since hired men watch for their wages. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-21/
- Pulpit: Kedar may stand for the northern Arabs generally. They lived in tents and villages and owned many flocks. They appear in Ashurbanipal's war records. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/21.htm
